title: Service mesh: Envoy, Istio, Linkerd and Cilium
intro: Part 10 gave you Services and a Gateway, and Parts 12 to 14 showed you metrics, logs and traces. This part is about the calls between your services: timeouts, retries, encryption with identity, traffic splits and per-call metrics. Day 58 builds the intuition with one Envoy proxy that you configure by hand and break on purpose. Day 59 runs Istio, and Day 60 compares Linkerd, Cilium and Consul and helps you decide whether you need a mesh at all.

lessons.title: Why a service mesh: proxies, sidecars and Envoy
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain which problems a proxy solves between services, read and change an Envoy config made of listeners, routes and clusters, and inspect a running Envoy through its admin port.

guess.q: Your app calls `http://orders/`. You add an Envoy sidecar to its Pod. What must change in the app so its calls go through the proxy?
options: The URL must point at the proxy, such as `localhost:15001`
Nothing: rules in the Pod's network send the traffic there
The app must load an Envoy client library at startup
The app must set the `HTTP_PROXY` environment variable
guess.why: A sidecar mesh writes packet rules (iptables) inside the Pod's network, so every connection in and out lands on the proxy first. The app keeps calling `http://orders/` and never notices.

terms.plain: A program that receives a request meant for someone else and makes the real request on the caller's behalf.
A helper container that runs in the same Pod as the app and shares its network.
The proxies that carry the real traffic between services.
The program that configures all the proxies and usually hands out their certificates.
An address and port where Envoy accepts connections from clients.
A named group of upstream hosts for one service, which Envoy balances requests across.
The family of APIs a control plane uses to send Envoy new config while it runs.
Envoy watching real answers and taking a host out of the pool after it fails too often.

sections.h: The problems that live between services
sections.body:
Inside one program, a function call returns or throws. Between two services, a call can also hang, time out after the work was already done, hit a copy that is shutting down, or reach the wrong version. Day 44 called this east-west traffic: calls between Services inside the cluster.

Picture a checkout service that calls a fraud check over HTTP. Before that call is safe in production, somebody has to decide:
- How long to wait before giving up. That is the timeout.
- Whether to try again, how often, and only for requests that are safe to repeat (Day 11 explained idempotent methods).
- Whether the call is encrypted, and how the fraud check knows the caller really is checkout.
- How to send 10% of calls to a new version of the fraud check.
- How many calls failed and how slow they were, for each pair of services.

None of this is business logic, and every service needs all of it. Left alone, each team solves it a little differently: one retries five times and another never, one waits 30 seconds and another 1. Those differences tend to surface during an outage, when they are hardest to untangle.

sections.h: A library in every app, or a proxy next to it
sections.body:
The first way to solve the list is a library inside every app. On the JVM you might use Resilience4j for retries and circuit breakers (which stop calling a service that keeps failing), plus your own TLS setup and a metrics library. Nothing extra sits on the network path, so it is fast. The costs arrive later:
- Each language needs its own library, and they never behave quite the same.
- A fix in the library means rebuilding and redeploying every service.
- The settings live in each app's code, so nobody can see them all in one place.

The second way moves the work out of the app into a proxy that runs next to it. The app makes a plain HTTP call. The proxy adds the timeout, the retry, the encryption and the metrics, and a second proxy on the receiving side does the same for incoming calls. The two proxies use mutual TLS (mTLS), the TLS of Day 11 with both sides showing a certificate, so each knows who the other is. Day 59 sets it up. Envoy's own docs give two reasons for this design: it works with any language, and you can upgrade the proxies without touching the apps.

A **service mesh** is the second way at scale: a proxy next to every service, plus one control plane that configures all of them. The proxies form the data plane. The price is an extra hop on every call, and CPU and memory for every proxy. Day 60 measures it.

One idea from Day 11 matters here. An L4 proxy sees TCP connections: addresses, ports and bytes. An L7 proxy reads each HTTP request: method, path, headers and status code. Retrying on a 503, routing by header and counting errors per request all need L7.

sections.h: Follow one request through Envoy
sections.body:
Envoy is an L7 proxy written in C++. It started at Lyft and is a graduated CNCF project, and you met it on Day 44 inside Envoy Gateway. Istio's debugging tools print Envoy's vocabulary back at you, so it pays to learn it once.

Start with two directions. Downstream is the side that sends requests to Envoy, such as curl. Upstream is the side Envoy sends them on to, such as hello-devops. Now follow one `curl localhost:10000/` through the lab's `envoy.yaml`:
1. A listener accepts the TCP connection. Ours is called `ingress` and listens on port 10000.
2. The listener runs its filter chain. Network filters work on raw bytes, and ours has one: the HTTP connection manager, or HCM.
3. The HCM turns bytes into HTTP requests and runs the HTTP filters in order. Ours are a fault filter, switched off until Day 59, and the router, which must come last.
4. The router looks up the route table. A virtual host matches the `Host` header, and `*` matches any. Inside it, the first route whose `match` fits wins.
5. The route names a cluster, or several with weights. Ours sends 90 to `hello_v1` and 10 to `hello_v2`.
6. The cluster's load balancer picks one endpoint, a single address and port such as `v1a:8000`, and sends the request over a pooled connection, one that Envoy keeps open and reuses.

Many of Envoy's features are filters: plug-in steps that see the traffic, may change or answer it, and pass it on. An Envoy that only proxies L4 holds the TCP proxy filter where ours holds the HCM, and never parses HTTP. The router comes last because it is the filter that sends the request upstream, so nothing after it would run.

An Envoy cluster has nothing to do with a Kubernetes cluster. It is a group of upstream hosts for one service. The lab lists host names such as `v1a`, and `type: STRICT_DNS` makes Envoy look them up in Compose's DNS (Day 20). Each of these objects is separate in the config. That lets a control plane change a route without touching a listener, or add an endpoint without touching a route.

sections.h: Timeouts, retries and spotting a sick host
sections.body:
Envoy's defaults are not what you want between services. A route waits 15 seconds, and it never retries until you say so. The lab sets both on purpose:
- `timeout: 3s` on the route is the budget for the whole request, retries included.
- `retry_policy` retries on `5xx,reset,connect-failure` (an error status, a dropped connection or a failed connect), at most twice, with `per_try_timeout: 1s` each.
- The `previous_hosts` predicate makes each retry pick a different host than the one that just failed.

Retries hide failures, and that is both their use and their danger. If each hop in a chain of three retries twice, one user request can become 27 calls to the last service, just when it is struggling. Retry only requests that are safe to repeat, keep the count low, and give each try its own timeout.

Envoy has two ways to notice a sick host. An active health check sends its own request, here `GET /healthz` every 5 seconds. Outlier detection is passive: it watches the real answers and ejects a host after `consecutive_5xx: 3`, three errors in a row. An ejected host is skipped for `base_ejection_time` (30 seconds here), and for longer each time it is ejected again. They see different things. In the worked example, one copy of the app loses its Redis: `/healthz` still says ok, but real requests fail, and only outlier detection notices.

Circuit breakers are the third tool. In Envoy they are limits per cluster on connections, waiting requests, parallel requests and parallel retries, by default 1024, 1024, 1024 and 3. Past a limit, Envoy answers 503 at once instead of letting a queue grow. A growing queue is how one slow service makes its callers slow too, because their threads and connections all sit waiting. Istio calls connection limits plus outlier detection circuit breaking, so you will hear the word for both.

sections.h: Static config, xDS and the control plane
sections.body:
The lab's `envoy.yaml` is static config. Everything is in one file, and a change means restarting Envoy. That is fine for one proxy in front of three containers that never move.

Kubernetes is the opposite. Pods start and stop all day, each with a new IP (Day 41), and a mesh may have hundreds of Envoys that must learn about every change within seconds. So Envoy can also fetch its config from a server while it runs, over gRPC (a remote-call protocol on HTTP/2). Envoy still starts from a small static file, the bootstrap, which says where that server is. The rest arrives over APIs called xDS, one for each kind of object:
- LDS, the listener discovery service, sends listeners.
- RDS sends route tables.
- CDS sends clusters.
- EDS sends endpoints: the Pod IPs behind each cluster. They change most often.
- SDS sends secrets, meaning TLS certificates and keys.

The x stands for any of these letters. Order matters: a route that names a cluster Envoy has not received yet sends its traffic nowhere. So many control planes send everything over one stream, called ADS (the aggregated discovery service), clusters before the routes that use them.

The server on the other end is the control plane. It watches the Kubernetes API for Services, EndpointSlices and your routing objects, turns them into Envoy objects and pushes them to every proxy. In Istio that is istiod; in Envoy Gateway it is the controller from Day 44. If the control plane goes down, the proxies keep serving with the last config they received. You only lose the ability to change it.

The admin interface shows what a running Envoy really has. `/config_dump` prints the live config, `/clusters` lists every host with its health, and `/stats` has counters for nearly everything. In the lab the dump lists our clusters under `static_clusters`. In an Istio sidecar the same dump fills `dynamic_active_clusters`, and `istioctl proxy-config` (Day 59) reads it for you.

sections.h: How traffic reaches the proxy: sidecars, nodes and ambient
sections.body:
A proxy only helps if traffic passes through it. In the lab you send requests to port 10000 by hand. In a mesh nobody changes the app's URLs, so the traffic has to be caught on its way.

In sidecar mode the proxy is an extra container in every Pod. The containers of a Pod share one network (Day 39), so the proxy can see the app's traffic. Before the app starts, an init container or a CNI plugin on the node writes iptables rules inside the Pod's network. They are the same kernel packet rules kube-proxy writes (Day 41). Istio's rules send outgoing connections to Envoy on port 15001 and incoming ones to port 15006. The app still calls `http://fraud-check/`, and the kernel quietly hands the connection to Envoy.

So how does Envoy know where the app meant to go? The kernel remembers the original address of every redirected connection, and Envoy reads it back. The rules also skip traffic sent by the proxy's own user (ID 1337 in Istio). Otherwise Envoy's outgoing calls would loop straight back into Envoy.

Sidecars used to start and stop awkwardly. The app could start before its proxy, and a Job never finished because the proxy kept running. Kubernetes native sidecar containers (Day 39) fix this. A native sidecar is an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`: it starts before the app, keeps running, and stops after it. They are stable since Kubernetes 1.33, and Istio and Linkerd both use them by default now.

A sidecar per Pod is easy to reason about, but 200 Pods means 200 proxies with their own memory. Two other designs share proxies:
- A per-node proxy carries the traffic of every Pod on its node. Cilium runs Envoy this way for its HTTP features (Day 60).
- Istio's ambient mode splits the job in two. A small L4 proxy on each node, called ztunnel, encrypts traffic for every Pod. An Envoy called a waypoint handles HTTP, only where you ask for it (Day 59).

Shared proxies save memory. In exchange, a noisy neighbor can slow your traffic, and a broken node proxy hurts every Pod on that node.

sections.h: Where you will meet Envoy
sections.body:
Envoy shows up all over this part of the stack, usually hidden behind a friendlier API:
- Envoy Gateway runs it at the edge of the cluster, configured by the Gateway API (Day 44).
- Istio runs it as every sidecar, every waypoint and every Istio gateway (Day 59).
- Cilium runs one per node for HTTP-aware policy and routing (Day 60).
- Consul's service mesh uses Envoy sidecars (Day 60).

AWS App Mesh was Amazon's managed mesh built on Envoy. AWS ended its support on September 30, 2026, so treat any App Mesh setup you find as a migration; AWS points ECS users to ECS Service Connect. Linkerd is the odd one out: it uses its own proxy, written in Rust.

Since all of these generate Envoy config, today's skills carry over. When a mesh misbehaves you end up in the same places: the listeners, the routes, the clusters with their health flags, and the stats.

lessons.analogy: A proxy next to each service works like the post room of an office building. Staff drop a letter in the out tray with just a name on it. The post room looks up the address, picks a courier, sends a second one if the first comes back empty-handed, and logs every delivery. Nobody upstairs has to learn how couriers work. A real post room adds hours and never opens the letters. Envoy adds well under a millisecond on a quiet machine, and it can read and change every header on the way through.

code.title: mesh/envoy/envoy.yaml
code.src:
# Envoy in front of two versions of hello-devops (Day 58).
# One listener on port 10000, one route table, two clusters:
#   hello_v1: two copies of version 1.0.0 (v1a, v1b)
#   hello_v2: one copy of the canary, version 2.0.0 (v2)
# About 9 in 10 requests go to hello_v1 and 1 in 10 to hello_v2.
# The admin interface on port 9901 shows the stats (/stats) and the hosts (/clusters).

admin:
  address:
    socket_address:
      address: 0.0.0.0 # inside the container; compose.yaml publishes it on 127.0.0.1 only
      port_value: 9901

# A runtime layer you can change through the admin interface while Envoy runs.
# Day 59 uses it to switch on fault injection with POST /runtime_modify.
layered_runtime:
  layers:
    - name: admin
      admin_layer: {}

static_resources:
  listeners:
    - name: ingress
      address:
        socket_address:
          address: 0.0.0.0
          port_value: 10000
      filter_chains:
        - filters:
            # The HTTP connection manager turns bytes into HTTP requests,
            # runs the HTTP filters and picks a route.
            - name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.http_connection_manager.v3.HttpConnectionManager
                stat_prefix: ingress_http
                access_log:
                  # One line per request on stdout: see it with docker compose logs envoy
                  - name: envoy.access_loggers.stdout
                    typed_config:
                      "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.access_loggers.stream.v3.StdoutAccessLog
                route_config:
                  name: hello_routes
                  virtual_hosts:
                    - name: hello
                      domains: ["*"] # any Host header
                      # Retries for every route in this virtual host.
                      retry_policy:
                        retry_on: "5xx,reset,connect-failure"
                        num_retries: 2
                        per_try_timeout: 1s
                        # Retry on a different host than the one that just failed.
                        retry_host_predicate:
                          - name: envoy.retry_host_predicates.previous_hosts
                            typed_config:
                              "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.retry.host.previous_hosts.v3.PreviousHostsPredicate
                        host_selection_retry_max_attempts: 3
                      routes:
                        # Testers can always reach the canary with the header "x-canary: always".
                        - match:
                            prefix: "/"
                            headers:
                              - name: x-canary
                                string_match:
                                  exact: always
                          route:
                            cluster: hello_v2
                            timeout: 3s
                        # Everyone else: a 90/10 split between the two clusters.
                        - match:
                            prefix: "/"
                          route:
                            weighted_clusters:
                              clusters:
                                - name: hello_v1
                                  weight: 90
                                - name: hello_v2
                                  weight: 10
                            timeout: 3s # the whole request, retries included
                http_filters:
                  # Fault injection, switched off (0 percent). Day 59 turns it on at run time.
                  - name: envoy.filters.http.fault
                    typed_config:
                      "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.fault.v3.HTTPFault
                      abort:
                        http_status: 503
                        percentage:
                          numerator: 0
                          denominator: HUNDRED
                      delay:
                        fixed_delay: 2s
                        percentage:
                          numerator: 0
                          denominator: HUNDRED
                  # The router sends the request to the cluster the route chose. It must be last.
                  - name: envoy.filters.http.router
                    typed_config:
                      "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.router.v3.Router

  clusters:
    - name: hello_v1
      type: STRICT_DNS # look up each host name and keep every address it returns
      connect_timeout: 1s
      lb_policy: ROUND_ROBIN
      load_assignment:
        cluster_name: hello_v1
        endpoints:
          - lb_endpoints:
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address: { address: v1a, port_value: 8000 }
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address: { address: v1b, port_value: 8000 }
      # Active health check: Envoy asks each host for /healthz every 5 seconds.
      health_checks:
        - timeout: 1s
          interval: 5s
          unhealthy_threshold: 2
          healthy_threshold: 1
          no_traffic_interval: 5s # the default is 60s while a cluster has had no traffic yet
          http_health_check:
            path: /healthz
      # Passive health check: watch real answers and eject a host after 3 errors in a row.
      outlier_detection:
        consecutive_5xx: 3
        interval: 5s
        base_ejection_time: 30s
        max_ejection_percent: 50 # the default is 10%, which with 2 hosts ejects nobody
        # /healthz only proves the process is up. Do not let it undo an ejection.
        successful_active_health_check_uneject_host: false
      # Circuit breakers: limits that make Envoy fail fast instead of queueing forever.
      circuit_breakers:
        thresholds:
          - max_connections: 100
            max_pending_requests: 50
            max_requests: 100
            max_retries: 3

    - name: hello_v2
      type: STRICT_DNS
      connect_timeout: 1s
      lb_policy: ROUND_ROBIN
      load_assignment:
        cluster_name: hello_v2
        endpoints:
          - lb_endpoints:
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address: { address: v2, port_value: 8000 }
      health_checks:
        - timeout: 1s
          interval: 5s
          unhealthy_threshold: 2
          healthy_threshold: 1
          no_traffic_interval: 5s # the default is 60s while a cluster has had no traffic yet
          http_health_check:
            path: /healthz
      outlier_detection:
        consecutive_5xx: 3
        interval: 5s
        base_ejection_time: 30s
        max_ejection_percent: 50
        successful_active_health_check_uneject_host: false
      circuit_breakers:
        thresholds:
          - max_connections: 100
            max_pending_requests: 50
            max_requests: 100
            max_retries: 3

# Day 58: Envoy in front of two versions of hello-devops.
# Needs the image hello-devops:1.0.0 (Day 19). If you do not have it:
#   docker build -t hello-devops:1.0.0 ../..
# Start:  docker compose up -d
# Proxy:  curl -s localhost:10000/
# Admin:  curl -s localhost:9901/clusters
# Stop:   docker compose down
name: mesh-envoy

services:
  envoy:
    image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.40.2
    volumes:
      - ./envoy.yaml:/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml:ro
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:10000:10000" # the proxy: send your requests here
      - "127.0.0.1:9901:9901" # the admin interface has no login, so keep it on localhost
    depends_on:
      - v1a
      - v1b
      - v2

  # Version 1: two copies that share one Redis for the visit counter.
  v1a:
    image: hello-devops:1.0.0
    pull_policy: never # a local image you built; never look for it on Docker Hub
    environment:
      APP_VERSION: "1.0.0"
      REDIS_HOST: redis

  # The second copy of version 1 has its own Redis, so you can break this one copy on
  # purpose: docker compose stop redis-b. Its /healthz stays 200, but / starts to fail.
  v1b:
    image: hello-devops:1.0.0
    pull_policy: never
    environment:
      APP_VERSION: "1.0.0"
      REDIS_HOST: redis-b

  # Version 2: the canary.
  v2:
    image: hello-devops:1.0.0
    pull_policy: never
    environment:
      APP_VERSION: "2.0.0"
      GREETING: "Hello from the canary!"
      REDIS_HOST: redis

  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine

  redis-b:
    image: redis:8-alpine

lessons.mistake: Turning on generous retries without a per-try timeout is how a slow service gets pushed over. Every failed call comes back two or three times, and the extra load arrives just when the service is weakest. Without a per-try timeout, one slow attempt can also use up the whole request budget, so the retry never happens. Allow one or two retries, set `per_try_timeout` well below the route `timeout`, and retry only requests that are safe to repeat.
lessons.real_world: After a deploy, one of five copies of a payment adapter starts timing out while its health endpoint still says ok. Without outlier detection, every fifth checkout waits three seconds and then fails. With it, the proxy stops sending traffic to that copy after three errors, and the dashboard shows one ejection instead of a wall of timeouts. Few teams write Envoy config by hand for this. They set the same numbers through Istio or Envoy Gateway objects, and read them back through the admin port when something looks wrong.

task.title: Tune the proxy, then watch a timeout fire
steps: Start the Day 58 lab and confirm the 90/10 split with a loop of 200 requests.
Change the weights in `envoy.yaml` to 50 and 50, run `docker compose restart envoy`, and count again.
Add a route above the others that sends `/healthz` (an exact path) to `hello_v1` only.
Call `/healthz` 20 times and check in `/clusters` that `rq_total` for the `hello_v2` host does not grow.
Freeze the canary with `docker compose pause v2`. Send 20 requests and print each status code and total time.
Find the failed requests in `docker compose logs envoy` and read their response flags. Then read `upstream_rq_per_try_timeout` and `upstream_rq_retry` for `hello_v2` in `/stats`.
Run `docker compose unpause v2`, put the weights back to 90 and 10, and commit `mesh/envoy` to your repo.
hints: A route's `match` can use `path: /healthz` for an exact path. Routes are tried from top to bottom, so the specific one goes first.
`hello_v2` has one host. A retry has nowhere else to go, and outlier detection with `max_ejection_percent: 50` cannot eject the only host.
In the access log, the field after the status code is the response flags. `UT` means the upstream request timed out.
task.done_when: You are done when the 50/50 loop shows about 100 of each version, `/healthz` never reaches `hello_v2`, and you can explain why about half the requests ended in 504 after 3 seconds while v2 was paused.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how one request travels through Envoy and how Envoy decides a host is sick. Mention listener, route, cluster and outlier detection.
explain_back.answer: A listener accepts the connection on a port, and its HTTP connection manager turns the bytes into requests and runs the HTTP filters. The router matches each request against the route table, and the matching route picks a cluster, here with weights of 90 and 10. The cluster's load balancer picks one healthy endpoint and sends the request there. Active health checks call a path like `/healthz` on a timer. Outlier detection watches the real answers and ejects a host after a few errors in a row, so a host that is up but broken still gets removed.

recap: Timeouts, retries, mTLS, traffic splits and per-call metrics are needed by every service, so they belong in shared infrastructure.
A mesh puts a proxy next to every service (the data plane) and one control plane in charge of them.
In Envoy, a listener accepts, the HTTP connection manager runs filters, a route picks a cluster and the cluster picks an endpoint.
Health checks probe hosts, outlier detection watches real traffic, and circuit breakers fail fast. Keep retries few and short.
xDS (LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS, SDS) changes Envoy's config while it runs; the admin port shows what it really has.
Sidecars catch traffic with iptables rules in the Pod; per-node and ambient designs share proxies to save memory.

check.q: An Envoy cluster has three hosts. One starts answering 500 to real requests while its `/healthz` keeps answering 200. Which feature takes it out of the pool?
options: Active health checking on `/healthz`
Outlier detection on consecutive 5xx
The route's `timeout` setting
A higher `max_connections` limit
check.why: Outlier detection judges the real answers; the health check only proves that `/healthz` works.

check.q: A gateway calls service A, A calls B, and B calls C. Each of the three hops makes up to three tries (one call plus two retries). C is down. How many calls can one user request cause at C?
options: 3 calls
9 calls
27 calls
81 calls
check.why: Each hop multiplies the one below it: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls land on C.

check.q: You add a route to a static `envoy.yaml`, save the file, and Envoy keeps serving the old routes. What is the most likely reason?
options: Static config is read at startup, so Envoy needs a restart
Routes can only arrive over EDS, never from a file
The admin port blocks changes while it is open
Envoy loads new routes only after a health check passes
check.why: A static file is loaded when Envoy starts; changes without a restart need xDS from a control plane.

interview.q: What is a service mesh, and what problem does it solve?
interview.a: A service mesh is a set of proxies next to every service, plus a control plane that configures them. It moves the network concerns of service-to-service calls out of application code: timeouts, retries, mTLS with workload identity, traffic splitting and per-call metrics. Every service gets the same behavior in any language, and the platform team can change it without redeploying apps. The price is an extra hop per call, CPU and memory for the proxies, and one more system to run and debug.

interview.q: Explain Envoy's listeners, routes, clusters and endpoints.
interview.a: A listener is an address and port where Envoy accepts connections, with a chain of filters. For HTTP, the HTTP connection manager parses requests and passes them through HTTP filters, ending with the router. The router matches each request against a route table, and the matching route names a cluster, or several with weights. A cluster is a group of upstream hosts with a load balancing policy, health checks and outlier detection, and each endpoint is one address and port in it. A control plane can update each layer on its own over LDS, RDS, CDS and EDS.

interview.q: What is the difference between the data plane and the control plane?
interview.a: The data plane is the set of proxies that carry every request: sidecars, waypoints or node proxies. The control plane carries no user traffic. It watches the platform, turns your config into proxy config, pushes it over xDS and usually signs certificates. If it fails, the proxies keep serving with their last config, and you cannot change anything until it is back.

deeper.body:
Two Envoy defaults surprised me while testing this lab, and both are worth knowing before you meet them at work.

The first run looked broken in `/clusters`. Every host carried the flag `/failed_active_hc`, yet every request worked. Two things were going on:
1. Envoy ran its first health checks the moment it started, while gunicorn in the app containers was still booting. They failed with a network error.
2. A cluster that has had no traffic yet is checked only every `no_traffic_interval`, which is 60 seconds by default. So the hosts stayed marked unhealthy for a whole minute after the apps were up.

Requests still worked because of the panic threshold. When fewer than 50% of a cluster's hosts are healthy, Envoy stops trusting the health flags and balances across all hosts. The reasoning is that a broken health check should not take down a service whose hosts are fine. You can change the threshold, or tell Envoy to fail all traffic in panic, in the cluster's load balancing settings. The lab sets `no_traffic_interval: 5s`, so the flags turn healthy within seconds.

The second surprise was ejection. Outlier detection never ejects more than `max_ejection_percent` of a cluster, and the default is 10%. In a cluster of two hosts, 10% is less than one host, so nobody is ever ejected. That is why the lab sets 50%. The hands-on shows the same rule from the other side: `hello_v2` has one host, so it is never ejected, and Envoy keeps sending it traffic while it times out.

Put together, these rules show a design choice. Envoy would rather send traffic to hosts that might be sick than send it nowhere. That is usually right, but a small cluster gets little protection from outlier detection. Run at least three copies of anything that matters, and look at `/clusters` before you trust a dashboard.

The [outlier detection](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/outlier) and [health checking](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/health_checking) pages of the Envoy docs list every setting with its default.

sections.h: One control plane, two kinds of data plane
sections.body:
Istio is a service mesh built on Envoy, and Day 58 already gave you most of its moving parts. The control plane is one program, istiod, with three jobs:
- It watches the Kubernetes API and your Istio and Gateway API objects, and turns them into listeners, routes, clusters and endpoints for every proxy, sent over xDS.
- It runs a certificate authority (a CA, the signer of certificates from Day 11) that gives every workload a short-lived certificate, valid for 24 hours by default.
- It runs the webhook that injects sidecars into new Pods.

That webhook is a mutating admission webhook, a Kubernetes hook for changing objects before they are stored. The API server sends each new Pod to istiod first, and istiod adds the Envoy container. Your Deployment's YAML never mentions the sidecar.

The data plane comes in two modes. One mesh can mix them, but each namespace should use one.

Sidecar mode is the original design, used since 2017. Every Pod gets an Envoy, and every call passes through two of them, the caller's and the receiver's. Each proxy handles both L4 and L7, so every feature works everywhere. The cost grows with the mesh: each sidecar is sized for its own Pod's busiest moment, and joining or upgrading means restarting every Pod.

**Ambient mode** splits the work into two layers. ztunnel, a proxy written in Rust, runs once per node. It encrypts and authenticates the traffic of every Pod on its node and enforces L4 rules, but never parses HTTP. For HTTP features you add a waypoint: an Envoy that runs as its own Deployment, usually one per namespace. Traffic between ztunnels and waypoints travels in an mTLS tunnel called HBONE (HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment), on port 15008. Most calls only need encryption and identity, which are cheap, so you pay for HTTP parsing only where you add a waypoint.

Ambient mode became generally available in Istio 1.24, in November 2024. Istio's page comparing the two modes lists it as Stable for a single cluster, and multi-cluster ambient is Beta. Istio 1.31, released in August 2026, is the current version as I write this. The comparison page also quotes Istio's latency tests, at p90 and p99:
- 0.63 to 0.88 ms per call with sidecars.
- 0.16 to 0.20 ms with ztunnel alone.
- 0.40 to 0.50 ms through a waypoint.

sections.h: Install on kind and join a namespace
sections.body:
On a Mac, `brew install istioctl` gets you the CLI. Istio's download script works too, and also brings the sample apps. istioctl installs Istio from a profile, a named set of settings:
- `default`: istiod plus an ingress gateway, the starting point for production.
- `demo`: more features and heavy logging, for tutorials only.
- `minimal`: istiod alone. The lab uses it, because the Gateway API creates gateways when you ask for one.
- `ambient`: istiod, ztunnel and the Istio CNI node agent, which sets up rules that send each Pod's traffic to ztunnel.

Install the Gateway API CRDs first, because Istio reads them. Istio 1.31's docs install Gateway API v1.6.0. Version 1.7.0 is out, and Envoy Gateway from Day 44 brings its own copy, so check which version a cluster already has before you apply another.

Then decide how each namespace joins the mesh:
- Sidecar mode: `kubectl label namespace hello-mesh istio-injection=enabled`. Only Pods created after the label get a sidecar, so restart your Deployments. Since Istio 1.27 the proxy is a native sidecar, an init container that keeps running.
- Ambient mode: `kubectl label namespace hello-mesh istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient`. ztunnel takes over the running Pods at once, with no restart and no extra container. The CNI node agent adds redirect rules inside each running Pod's network, and the Pod spec never changes. When you need HTTP features, add a waypoint with `istioctl waypoint apply -n hello-mesh --enroll-namespace`.

Never put both labels on one namespace. If you do, sidecar mode wins for those Pods.

sections.h: Routing: the Gateway API first, then the Istio APIs you will still meet
sections.body:
Istio has its own routing objects, older than the Gateway API, and the project says it intends to make the Gateway API its default. For new work, write Gateway API objects. Traffic from outside enters through a Gateway with HTTPRoutes attached (Day 44). Traffic inside the mesh uses an HTTPRoute whose `parentRef` is a Service instead of a Gateway. Day 60 explains that pattern, called GAMMA.

The lab's `httproute-canary.yaml` attaches to the `hello-devops` Service. istiod turns it into Envoy routes in the client's sidecar, which applies them to every call to `http://hello-devops`:
- A request with the header `x-canary: always` goes to the canary.
- Everything else is split 90 to 10 by weight.
- `timeouts.request: 3s` caps each request.

Older Istio setups use Istio's own objects, and you will meet them at work:
- VirtualService: routing rules for a host, with retries, timeouts, header matches and fault injection.
- DestinationRule: what happens after routing picked a destination. Connection limits, outlier detection, TLS settings and subsets (named groups of Pods by label, such as `version: v2`) live here.
- Istio's Gateway, in the `networking.istio.io` group: settings for an ingress proxy you deployed yourself. It is a different object from the Gateway API's Gateway, despite the name.

Retries show where the two APIs still differ. The Standard channel of Gateway API v1.6.0 has no retry field, and v1.7.0 added one, so the lab puts retries in the VirtualService. Do not let an HTTPRoute and a VirtualService both route the same Service. The lab deletes one before it applies the other, so you always know which rules are live.

sections.h: Breaking things on purpose: faults and circuit breakers
sections.body:
How does your app behave when a dependency is slow or failing? Waiting for an outage to find out is expensive. Fault injection causes the failure on purpose, in a share of requests you choose.

A VirtualService rule can add two kinds of fault:
- A delay holds the request for a while, say 2 seconds, before sending it on.
- An abort answers at once with a status such as 503, without calling the service at all.

Each fault has a `percentage`, so you can hurt 1 request in 5 and leave the others alone. The lab's file only injects faults into requests that carry `x-fault: on`, which keeps normal traffic safe. Istio switches off timeouts and retries on a rule that injects faults, so healthy traffic gets a second rule with a 3-second timeout and two retries. The fault happens in the caller's sidecar, which is exactly where your own timeout and retry code would notice it.

Circuit breaking lives in a DestinationRule, and it maps one to one onto Day 58's Envoy settings:
- `connectionPool.tcp.maxConnections` and `connectionPool.http.http1MaxPendingRequests` become Envoy circuit breakers. Over the limit, the caller gets a 503 at once.
- `outlierDetection.consecutive5xxErrors`, `interval`, `baseEjectionTime` and `maxEjectionPercent` become Envoy outlier detection.

Istio even keeps Envoy's stat names. Its circuit breaking task reads `upstream_rq_pending_overflow` for a cluster called `outbound|8000||httpbin.default.svc.cluster.local`: direction, port, subset and host, in that order.

sections.h: Identity and mutual TLS
sections.body:
Day 11 showed TLS in which only the server proves who it is. In mutual TLS both sides present a certificate, so the server also learns who is calling. Istio gives every workload that certificate automatically.

The identity comes from the Pod's ServiceAccount, the identity for programs from Day 46. Every Pod runs as one, `default` unless you name another. Istio writes it as a SPIFFE ID. SPIFFE, the Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone, is a standard format for workload names: `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/hello-mesh/sa/client` is ServiceAccount `client` in namespace `hello-mesh`, in the trust domain `cluster.local`. That is why the lab gives each Deployment its own ServiceAccount. Workloads that share one also share an identity.

A sidecar gets its certificate in four steps:
1. The Istio agent next to Envoy creates a private key and a signing request.
2. It sends the request to istiod, with the Pod's ServiceAccount token as proof.
3. istiod checks the token and signs a certificate valid for 24 hours.
4. The agent hands key and certificate to Envoy over SDS, the secret API from Day 58, and renews them before they expire.

The short life limits the damage of a stolen key, and nobody rotates certificates by hand. The SPIFFE ID sits inside the certificate, so the receiving proxy learns who is calling from the handshake itself, not from anything the app sent.

PeerAuthentication says what a workload accepts:
- PERMISSIVE, the default, accepts mTLS and plain text. Meshed callers already use mTLS, and callers outside the mesh still work.
- STRICT accepts mTLS only, and plain-text callers are refused.
- DISABLE turns mTLS off. Avoid it.

In PERMISSIVE mode one port takes both. The receiving Envoy looks at the first bytes of each connection, and a TLS handshake is easy to tell from plain text. On the calling side, istiod tells each sidecar which destinations have a proxy, and the sidecar uses mTLS to those by itself.

Move to STRICT in steps: start PERMISSIVE, check that every caller of a namespace is in the mesh, then switch that namespace. In the lab, a Pod in the `outside` namespace can call hello-devops until you apply `peerauthentication.yaml`. After that the call fails, and curl exits with code 56: the connection was cut before any HTTP answer arrived.

sections.h: AuthorizationPolicy: who may call what
sections.body:
With mTLS on, every request arrives with a verified caller identity, and AuthorizationPolicy can use it. A policy has three parts:
- `selector`, or `targetRefs` in ambient mode: the workloads it protects.
- `action`: ALLOW, DENY, AUDIT (log only) or CUSTOM (ask an outside service).
- `rules`: `from` the caller (principals, namespaces, IP ranges) and `to` the operation (methods, paths, ports).

Istio checks CUSTOM policies first, then DENY, then ALLOW. A workload with no policy allows everything. Once any ALLOW policy selects it, every request that no ALLOW rule matches is refused with 403 and the text `RBAC: access denied`. So an ALLOW rule written for one new caller can lock out every other caller of that workload.

The lab has two policies for both app versions:
1. `deny-metrics` refuses `/metrics` to every namespace except `monitoring`. `notNamespaces` reads the caller's namespace from its certificate, so a forged header cannot get around it.
2. `allow-client-get` lets only `cluster.local/ns/hello-mesh/sa/client` in, only with GET, and only on `/`, `/healthz` and `/readyz`. A principal is the SPIFFE ID without `spiffe://`.

In ambient mode, where the policy runs matters. ztunnel sees connections, so it can enforce identity and port rules but not paths or methods. A policy with HTTP rules has to be attached to a waypoint with `targetRefs`. If you write it with a `selector` instead, ztunnel enforces it and, to fail safe, treats it as a DENY. The lab's `ambient/authorizationpolicy.yaml` is the waypoint version.

sections.h: Debugging and observing: istioctl, Prometheus, Kiali and traces
sections.body:
Most Istio problems are config that did not do what you meant. istioctl shows what each proxy really received:
- `istioctl analyze` checks your objects for known mistakes, such as a route to a missing Service. With `--use-kube=false` it checks files, with no cluster.
- `istioctl proxy-status` lists every proxy and whether it has istiod's latest config.
- `istioctl proxy-config listener`, `route`, `cluster`, `endpoint` and `secret` print one part of a proxy's live config, in Day 58's vocabulary. `secret` shows the workload certificate and its expiry.
- `istioctl dashboard envoy deployment/client -n hello-mesh` opens that sidecar's Envoy admin page, with the same `/clusters` and `/stats` as yesterday.
- In ambient mode, `istioctl ztunnel-config workload` shows what ztunnel knows about each Pod.

Every proxy exports Prometheus metrics, and the one to start with is `istio_requests_total`, a counter labeled with source, destination and response code. The PromQL from Day 51 works on it unchanged. Kiali reads those metrics and draws a live graph of who calls whom, with error rates on the edges. Istio's sample addons install Prometheus and Kiali in two commands, listed in the lab's README.

Traces need one thing from you. The proxies can create a span for every hop, but a proxy cannot tell which outgoing call belongs to which incoming request inside your app. Your app must copy the trace headers from the request it received onto the requests it sends: the context propagation of Day 57. OpenTelemetry instrumentation does it for you. Without it, Jaeger shows one short trace per hop instead of one trace per user request.

lessons.analogy: Workload identity in Istio works like staff badges in an office tower. A badge office (istiod) prints every employee a badge that is valid for one day, with their name and team on it. Door readers (the proxies) check the badge instead of the face, and a sign on each door says which teams may enter. In ambient mode one guard per floor (ztunnel) checks badges for everyone on that floor, and only rooms with special rules get their own doorman (a waypoint). A badge can be lent to a friend; a workload's key stays inside its proxy and is useless after a day.

worked.title: Fault injection by hand in Envoy, then the Istio way

steps.say: Start the Day 58 lab again. Its `envoy.yaml` already has a fault filter at 0 percent and a runtime layer. That layer holds values the admin port can change while Envoy runs, and the fault filter reads them on every request. Turn faults on while Envoy runs: abort 10% of requests with a 503 and delay 20% by 2 seconds. Envoy answers OK, and `/runtime` shows the new values.
steps.code:
$ docker compose up -d
$ curl -s -X POST 'localhost:9901/runtime_modify?fault.http.abort.abort_percent=10&fault.http.delay.fixed_delay_percent=20'
OK
$ curl -s localhost:9901/runtime | jq -c '.entries | with_entries(select(.key | startswith("fault"))) | map_values(.final_value)'
{"fault.http.abort.abort_percent":"10","fault.http.delay.fixed_delay_percent":"20"}

steps.say: Send 100 requests and keep each status code and total time. Six were aborted and 30 took more than 1.5 seconds. Each request rolls the dice on its own, so your counts will differ, and a few requests get both faults.
steps.code:
$ for i in $(seq 1 100); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' localhost:10000/; done > faults.txt
$ awk '{print $1}' faults.txt | sort | uniq -c
     94 200
      6 503
$ awk '$2 > 1.5' faults.txt | wc -l
30

steps.say: The access log explains each odd line. The field after the status code is the response flags: `FI` is an injected abort and `DI` an injected delay. The aborted request never reached a host, so its upstream host at the end is `-`. The delayed one took 2004 ms in total, of which the app spent 3 ms.
steps.code:
$ docker compose logs --no-log-prefix envoy | grep '" 503 FI ' | tail -1
[2026-11-07T17:50:22.307Z] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 503 FI 0 18 0 - "-" "curl/8.5.0" "b7cd01d9-8c59-4461-97ee-0868c8c7ce5f" "localhost:10000" "-"
$ docker compose logs --no-log-prefix envoy | grep '" 200 DI ' | tail -1
[2026-11-07T17:50:32.563Z] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 DI 0 81 2004 3 "-" "curl/8.5.0" "d1711511-dee2-41f7-86a7-1801c99089c7" "localhost:10000" "172.20.0.2:8000"

steps.say: Envoy counts every fault it injects. Check these counters whenever a fault test seems to change nothing: maybe the test never ran. Then switch the faults off again.
steps.code:
$ curl -s 'localhost:9901/stats?filter=^http\.ingress_http\.fault\.(aborts|delays)_injected$'
http.ingress_http.fault.aborts_injected: 6
http.ingress_http.fault.delays_injected: 30
$ curl -s -X POST 'localhost:9901/runtime_modify?fault.http.abort.abort_percent=0&fault.http.delay.fixed_delay_percent=0'
OK
$ docker compose down

steps.say: Now the Istio version. You never write the fault filter yourself there. You write a VirtualService rule, and istiod puts the same Envoy fault settings into the routes of every calling sidecar. This is the fault rule from the lab's `virtualservice-fault.yaml`. It only hurts requests with the header `x-fault: on`.
steps.code:
- match:
        - headers:
            x-fault:
              exact: "on"
      fault:
        delay:
          percentage:
            value: 50
          fixedDelay: 2s
        abort:
          percentage:
            value: 20
          httpStatus: 503

steps.say: Check Istio files before you go near a cluster. On your Mac, `istioctl analyze --use-kube=false *.yaml` runs Istio's own offline checks. The course checked the lab with kubeconform and JSON schemas made from the CRD files of Istio 1.31 and Gateway API v1.6.0. All 20 objects passed, and a one-letter typo in the DestinationRule was caught at once (error trimmed).
steps.code:
$ kubeconform -strict -summary -schema-location default \
    -schema-location 'schemas/{{.Group}}/{{.ResourceKind}}_{{.ResourceAPIVersion}}.json' *.yaml ambient/*.yaml
Summary: 20 resources found in 10 files - Valid: 20, Invalid: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
$ sed 's/consecutive5xxErrors/consecutive5xxError/' destinationrule.yaml > dr-typo.yaml
$ kubeconform -strict -schema-location default -schema-location 'schemas/{{.Group}}/{{.ResourceKind}}_{{.ResourceAPIVersion}}.json' dr-typo.yaml

code.title: mesh/istio/namespace.yaml
code.src:
# Two namespaces for the Istio lab (Day 59).
# hello-mesh: in the mesh. The label tells Istio to add an Envoy sidecar to every new Pod here.
#   Pods that already run get no sidecar until they restart.
# outside: not in the mesh. Use it to test what PeerAuthentication STRICT does to plain-text callers.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: hello-mesh
  labels:
    istio-injection: enabled
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: outside

code.title: mesh/istio/apps.yaml
code.src:
# hello-devops in the mesh (Day 59): version 1, a canary, and a client to call them from.
# Each app gets its own ServiceAccount, because Istio builds each workload's identity from it:
#   spiffe://cluster.local/ns/hello-mesh/sa/<service account name>
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello-mesh
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: hello-canary
  namespace: hello-mesh
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: client
  namespace: hello-mesh
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello-mesh
  labels:
    app: hello-devops
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-devops
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-devops # Istio uses app and version in its metrics
        version: v1
        app.kubernetes.io/part-of: hello-devops # the AuthorizationPolicy selects on this
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: hello-devops
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hello-devops:1.0.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent # use the image kind loaded; do not pull it
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: APP_VERSION
              value: "1.0.0"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-canary
  namespace: hello-mesh
  labels:
    app: hello-canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-canary
        version: v2
        app.kubernetes.io/part-of: hello-devops
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: hello-canary
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hello-devops:1.0.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: APP_VERSION
              value: "1.1.0-canary"
            - name: GREETING
              value: "Hello from the canary!"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello-mesh
  labels:
    app: hello-devops
spec:
  selector:
    app: hello-devops
  ports:
    - name: http # the name tells Istio this port speaks HTTP
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-canary
  namespace: hello-mesh
  labels:
    app: hello-canary
spec:
  selector:
    app: hello-canary
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
---
# A Pod that does nothing but wait, so you can run curl from inside the mesh:
#   kubectl exec -n hello-mesh deploy/client -- curl -s http://hello-devops/
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: client
  namespace: hello-mesh
  labels:
    app: client
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: client
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: client
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: client
      containers:
        - name: curl
          image: curlimages/curl:8.22.0
          command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 10m
              memory: 16Mi
            limits:
              memory: 64Mi
code.run: kind load docker-image hello-devops:1.0.0 --name mesh && kubectl apply -f apps.yaml

code.title: mesh/istio/httproute-canary.yaml
code.src:
# A canary inside the mesh, written with the Gateway API (Day 59).
# The parentRef is a Service, not a Gateway: the route applies to every meshed call
# to http://hello-devops (the GAMMA way, Day 60). Envoy on the caller's side does the split.
# Uses only Standard-channel fields of Gateway API v1.6.0, the version Istio 1.31's docs install.
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: hello-devops-canary
  namespace: hello-mesh
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - group: "" # "" is the core API group, where Service lives
      kind: Service
      name: hello-devops
      port: 80
  rules:
    # Rule 1: testers who send "x-canary: always" always reach the canary.
    - matches:
        - headers:
            - name: x-canary
              value: always
      backendRefs:
        - name: hello-canary
          port: 80
    # Rule 2: everyone else. About 9 in 10 requests stay on version 1.
    - backendRefs:
        - name: hello-devops
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: hello-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 10
      timeouts:
        request: 3s # give up after 3 seconds and answer 504

code.title: mesh/istio/destinationrule.yaml
code.src:
# Circuit breaking for calls to hello-devops (Day 59).
# Istio turns this into the same Envoy settings you wrote by hand on Day 58:
#   connectionPool   -> circuit_breakers (fail fast when too many calls wait)
#   outlierDetection -> outlier_detection (eject a Pod after 3 errors in a row)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello-mesh
spec:
  host: hello-devops.hello-mesh.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 10 # at most 10 connections from each caller's proxy
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 5 # more than 5 waiting requests: answer 503 at once
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 10
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 3
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50 # never eject more than half the Pods

code.title: mesh/istio/peerauthentication.yaml
code.src:
# Mutual TLS for every workload in hello-mesh (Day 59).
# STRICT: accept only mTLS traffic from other mesh workloads. Plain text is refused.
# The default, with no policy, is PERMISSIVE: accept both mTLS and plain text.
# On a real system, run PERMISSIVE first, check that every caller uses mTLS, then switch.
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: hello-mesh
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

code.title: mesh/istio/authorizationpolicy.yaml
code.src:
# Who may call hello-devops and the canary (Day 59). Needs mTLS, because the caller's
# identity comes from its certificate.
# Istio checks DENY policies first, then ALLOW policies. Once any ALLOW policy selects
# a workload, every request that no ALLOW rule matches is refused with 403.

# 1. Deny /metrics to everyone outside the "monitoring" namespace.
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-metrics
  namespace: hello-mesh
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/part-of: hello-devops
  action: DENY
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            notNamespaces: ["monitoring"]
      to:
        - operation:
            paths: ["/metrics"]
---
# 2. Allow only the client's identity, only GET, only these paths.
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-client-get
  namespace: hello-mesh
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/part-of: hello-devops
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/hello-mesh/sa/client"]
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["GET"]
            paths: ["/", "/healthz", "/readyz"]

code.title: mesh/istio/virtualservice-fault.yaml
code.src:
# Fault injection with Istio's own routing API (Day 59).
# Only requests with the header "x-fault: on" get faults, so normal traffic is not hurt.
# Do not use this together with httproute-canary.yaml: delete that route first, so that
# only one routing API controls calls to hello-devops.
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello-mesh
spec:
  hosts:
    - hello-devops.hello-mesh.svc.cluster.local
  http:
    # Rule 1: test traffic. 1 in 2 requests waits 2 seconds; 1 in 5 gets a 503 at once.
    # Istio switches off timeouts and retries on a rule that injects faults.
    - match:
        - headers:
            x-fault:
              exact: "on"
      fault:
        delay:
          percentage:
            value: 50
          fixedDelay: 2s
        abort:
          percentage:
            value: 20
          httpStatus: 503
      route:
        - destination:
            host: hello-devops.hello-mesh.svc.cluster.local
            port:
              number: 80
    # Rule 2: everyone else, with a timeout and retries.
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: hello-devops.hello-mesh.svc.cluster.local
            port:
              number: 80
      timeout: 3s
      retries:
        attempts: 2
        perTryTimeout: 1s
        retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure
code.run: kubectl delete -f httproute-canary.yaml && kubectl apply -f virtualservice-fault.yaml

code.title: mesh/istio/ambient/namespace.yaml
code.src:
# Ambient variant (Day 59): use this instead of ../namespace.yaml.
# istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient puts every Pod here in the mesh through ztunnel, the
# per-node proxy. No sidecars, and Pods do not need a restart.
# istio.io/use-waypoint=waypoint sends traffic for this namespace's Services through the
# waypoint proxy in waypoint.yaml, which does the HTTP (L7) work.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: hello-mesh
  labels:
    istio.io/dataplane-mode: ambient
    istio.io/use-waypoint: waypoint
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: outside

code.title: mesh/istio/ambient/waypoint.yaml
code.src:
# A waypoint: an Envoy proxy that Istio runs for the hello-mesh namespace (ambient mode).
# This is the file that "istioctl waypoint generate --for service -n hello-mesh" prints.
# Same as: istioctl waypoint apply -n hello-mesh
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: waypoint
  namespace: hello-mesh
  labels:
    istio.io/waypoint-for: service # handle traffic sent to Services (the default)
spec:
  gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint
  listeners:
    - name: mesh
      port: 15008
      protocol: HBONE # Istio's mTLS tunnel between ztunnels and waypoints

code.title: mesh/istio/ambient/authorizationpolicy.yaml
code.src:
# Ambient variant of ../authorizationpolicy.yaml (Day 59).
# ztunnel cannot read HTTP, so a policy with paths or methods must be attached to the
# waypoint. targetRefs to a Service does that: the waypoint for that Service enforces it.
# A selector-based policy with HTTP rules would be enforced by ztunnel and turn into a DENY.
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-client-get
  namespace: hello-mesh
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: ""
      kind: Service
      name: hello-devops
    - group: ""
      kind: Service
      name: hello-canary
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/hello-mesh/sa/client"]
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["GET"]
            paths: ["/", "/healthz", "/readyz"]

lessons.mistake: Switching a namespace to `STRICT` before every caller is in the mesh breaks those callers at once. A scraper, a CronJob in another namespace or an old VM without a proxy starts failing, and the error looks like a network fault. Stay in PERMISSIVE, look in Istio's metrics or Kiali for plain-text traffic into the namespace, mesh those callers, and only then switch.
lessons.real_world: Rolling Istio out across a company's clusters usually happens namespace by namespace, in the same order. Metrics come first, because a graph of who calls whom finds forgotten dependencies within a day. Then mTLS in permissive mode, then strict, and only after that the traffic rules. App teams own their HTTPRoutes and fault tests, while the platform team owns istiod, its upgrades and the certificate authority.

task.title: Run the Istio lab on kind
steps: Give Docker Desktop at least 8 GB of memory, create a kind cluster named `mesh`, and install istioctl.
Follow `mesh/istio/README.md` to install the Gateway API CRDs and Istio with the `minimal` profile.
Load `hello-devops:1.0.0` into kind, apply `namespace.yaml` and `apps.yaml`, and confirm with `istioctl proxy-status` that every Pod has a proxy.
Apply the HTTPRoute and count the versions over 200 calls from the client Pod. Then send one call with `x-canary: always`.
From a Pod in the `outside` namespace, call hello-devops before and after you apply `peerauthentication.yaml`.
Apply `authorizationpolicy.yaml`. From the client, check that `/` answers 200 and `/metrics` answers 403.
Delete the HTTPRoute, apply `virtualservice-fault.yaml`, and send 20 calls with and 20 without `x-fault: on`.
Find the fault settings in `istioctl proxy-config route deployment/client -n hello-mesh -o json`, then delete the cluster.
hints: If `kubectl exec` picks the wrong container, add `-c curl`: the proxy is a second container in the Pod.
If a Pod has no sidecar, it was created before the namespace label. Run `kubectl rollout restart deployment -n hello-mesh`.
A 403 with `RBAC: access denied` comes from the proxy, so the app's logs show nothing for those calls.
task.done_when: You are done when about 9 in 10 of the client's calls reach version 1.0.0, the Pod in `outside` is refused under STRICT, and `/metrics` answers 403 to the client.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how two workloads in an Istio mesh know who the other is, and how you turn that into a rule. Mention ServiceAccount, SPIFFE ID, PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy.
explain_back.answer: Each workload's identity comes from its Kubernetes ServiceAccount, written as a SPIFFE ID such as spiffe://cluster.local/ns/hello-mesh/sa/client. The control plane, istiod, signs a certificate with that ID that lasts 24 hours, and the proxies on both sides present their certificates in a mutual TLS handshake. PeerAuthentication decides whether a workload also accepts plain text (PERMISSIVE) or only mTLS (STRICT). AuthorizationPolicy then allows or denies requests by that verified identity, and by namespace, method and path.

recap: istiod is the control plane: xDS config, workload certificates and sidecar injection.
Sidecar mode puts Envoy in every Pod; ambient mode uses ztunnel per node for L4 and waypoints for L7.
Ambient mode has been GA since Istio 1.24 and needs no Pod restarts; VirtualService on a waypoint is still Alpha.
Write new routes as Gateway API HTTPRoutes; DestinationRules still hold connection limits and outlier detection.
Identity comes from ServiceAccounts as SPIFFE IDs. Go PERMISSIVE, check every caller, then STRICT.
Once an ALLOW policy selects a workload, everything it does not allow gets a 403.

check.q: In ambient mode you add an AuthorizationPolicy with a `selector` that allows only `GET /orders`. No waypoint exists. What happens?
options: ztunnel enforces the path rule itself
Istio refuses the policy when you apply it
ztunnel cannot read paths, so it acts as a DENY
The policy is ignored and all traffic passes
check.why: ztunnel only sees connections, so a selector policy with HTTP rules fails safe and denies; attach it to a waypoint with `targetRefs`.

check.q: A DestinationRule sets `http1MaxPendingRequests: 1`. A load test fires 20 calls at once from a meshed client. What do many of them get?
options: A 503 from the caller's proxy, without waiting
A 429 from hello-devops itself
A longer wait, but every call succeeds
A TLS error, because the pool is full
check.why: Past the pending-request limit, Envoy's circuit breaker fails the call at once with a 503.

check.q: Deployments `billing` and `reports` both run as ServiceAccount `default`. An AuthorizationPolicy allows only billing's principal. What can `reports` do?
options: Nothing, because Istio tells them apart by Pod name
Call the service too, because they share one identity
Call it, but only over plain text
Call it, but only after a sidecar restart
check.why: The identity is the ServiceAccount, so two workloads that share one are the same principal to Istio.

interview.q: Sidecar mode or ambient mode: how would you choose?
interview.a: Ambient mode costs less: one ztunnel per node instead of an Envoy per Pod, no Pod restarts to join, and HTTP processing only where you add a waypoint. Istio's own tests also show lower latency for it. Sidecar mode is older and supports every feature, including multi-cluster at the Stable level, and it gives each workload its own keys. For a new single-cluster mesh I would start in ambient mode with L4 only. Then I would add waypoints where a team needs HTTP features, unless a feature I need is still missing there.

interview.q: How does Istio implement mutual TLS between services?
interview.a: Each workload gets an identity from its ServiceAccount, in SPIFFE format. The Istio agent next to the proxy asks istiod to sign a certificate for that identity, gets one valid for 24 hours, and hands it to Envoy over SDS. The proxies on both sides present certificates and check each other against the mesh's trust root. PeerAuthentication controls whether plain text is still accepted, and AuthorizationPolicy uses the verified identity to allow or deny calls.

interview.q: A request through the mesh returns 503. How do you find out whether the proxy or the app produced it?
interview.a: I check the proxy's access log first. Envoy's response flags tell you when the proxy answered by itself, such as UO for a circuit breaker overflow or UH for no healthy upstream. The commands `istioctl proxy-config cluster` and `endpoint` show whether the destination has healthy endpoints at all, and `istioctl analyze` catches routes to missing Services. If the proxy forwarded the request and the upstream answered 503, the app's own logs show it.

deeper.body:
Follow one call in ambient mode, from the `client` Pod to `hello-devops`, with a waypoint in place:
1. The client opens a plain TCP connection to the Service IP. It has no idea a mesh exists.
2. When the Pod joined the mesh, the Istio CNI node agent wrote redirect rules inside the Pod's network namespace. They send the connection to the ztunnel on the same node, which listens inside the Pod's namespace on ports 15001, 15006 and 15008.
3. ztunnel looks up the destination. The namespace uses a waypoint, so ztunnel sends the bytes to the waypoint instead of straight to a Pod.
4. The bytes travel inside HBONE, an HTTP CONNECT tunnel over mutual TLS on port 15008. ztunnel presents the client's certificate, so the waypoint knows the caller is `sa/client`.
5. The waypoint is a full Envoy. It parses HTTP, applies the HTTPRoute split and the AuthorizationPolicy, picks a hello-devops Pod, and opens a new HBONE tunnel to the ztunnel on that Pod's node.
6. That ztunnel checks its L4 policy, unwraps the tunnel and delivers plain TCP to the app in its Pod.

Without a waypoint, steps 3 to 5 disappear and the two ztunnels talk to each other directly. That is the cheap path: encryption, identity and L4 policy, with no HTTP parsing anywhere.

Two consequences matter in practice. The first is keys. Each ztunnel holds certificates only for the Pods on its own node, and an app container never sees a key. Istio's comparison page counts that as a security gain over sidecars. The second is that the waypoint label states an intent; it does not force anything. Istio's docs warn that traffic can bypass a waypoint, for example when the waypoint has no address yet. To make it mandatory, add a policy that ztunnel enforces on the workload and that allows only the waypoint's identity.

Istio 1.31 added an Alpha feature that applies the canary idea to the mesh itself: a Service can point at a primary and a canary waypoint, with a weight. You can roll out a new waypoint config to a few percent of connections before every caller gets it. The [ambient data plane page](https://istio.io/latest/docs/ambient/architecture/data-plane/) draws these paths, and the [waypoint page](https://istio.io/latest/docs/ambient/usage/waypoint/) covers the labels.

lessons.title: Linkerd, Cilium and choosing a mesh (or none)
lessons.goal: By the end you can compare Linkerd, Istio, Cilium and Consul, write one GAMMA route that works in more than one mesh, put numbers on what a mesh costs, and decide whether your system needs one.

guess.q: Cilium's service mesh is often called sidecar-free. Where does an HTTP retry or a path-based route actually run?
options: In eBPF programs inside the Linux kernel
In an Envoy proxy that runs once on each node
In the application's own container
In the Kubernetes API server
guess.why: eBPF handles L3 and L4 work in the kernel, but HTTP is parsed by Envoy. Cilium runs one Envoy per node, the `cilium-envoy` DaemonSet, for its L7 features.

terms.plain: Linkerd's sidecar proxy: a small proxy written in Rust, built only for service mesh work.
A frequent Linkerd build from the main branch, named like edge-26.11.1; the open source project ships only these.
The root certificate a mesh trusts; every workload certificate is signed under it.
Small programs that the Linux kernel runs safely, which Cilium uses to handle packets without a user-space proxy.
Cilium's tool that records the network flows between Pods so you can watch and search them.
The Gateway API's way to configure a mesh: routes attach to a Service instead of a Gateway.
A GAMMA route in the same namespace as its Service; it applies to callers from every namespace.

sections.h: Linkerd: a small proxy and few knobs
sections.body:
Linkerd's site calls it the first service mesh project, and it was the first mesh to graduate in the CNCF. Its goal is to do the common things with very little configuration.

The control plane has three parts:
- The destination service tells each proxy where a Service's endpoints are and which policies apply.
- The identity service is a certificate authority. It signs a certificate for each proxy, bound to the Pod's ServiceAccount, valid for 24 hours and rotated automatically.
- The proxy injector is a mutating webhook, like Istio's (Day 59). It adds the proxy to new Pods in namespaces annotated `linkerd.io/inject: enabled`.

The data plane is linkerd2-proxy, a micro-proxy written in Rust; Linkerd does not use Envoy. It runs as a sidecar in every Pod, and since Linkerd 2.20 it is a native sidecar by default. An init container, or Linkerd's CNI plugin, writes the iptables rules that send the Pod's traffic through it.

What you get before writing a single policy:
- mTLS for all TCP traffic between meshed Pods, from the moment they are meshed.
- Golden metrics for every workload: success rate, requests per second and latency, much like Day 49's golden signals.
- Load balancing per request, toward the fastest endpoints by a moving average of latency. Day 41's kube-proxy balances only connections, so one long-lived gRPC connection stays on one Pod.

The viz extension adds the tools to see it:
- `linkerd viz stat-outbound` prints a workload's calls by route and backend.
- `linkerd viz edges` shows which connections are secured.
- `linkerd viz tap` streams live requests, and `linkerd viz dashboard` opens a web UI.

Linkerd has stayed with sidecars: every meshed Pod has its own proxy.

sections.h: Linkerd's releases and license today
sections.body:
The Linkerd code is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. What changed in February 2024 is who builds the releases:
- The open source project publishes edge releases about once a week, named `edge-YY.M.N`. `edge-26.11.1` is the first edge release of November 2026. The project calls edge releases production ready and marks one as not recommended when a bug turns up.
- The project still announces versions such as 2.20 (June 2026), but it no longer publishes stable builds of them. Those come from vendors.
- Buoyant, the company that created Linkerd, sells Buoyant Enterprise for Linkerd (BEL). Its FAQ says companies with fewer than 50 employees may run it for free, in production too. Larger companies may evaluate it outside production and pay to run it in production.

For you as a learner nothing changes: the getting started guide installs the latest edge release, and so does the lab. At work, somebody has to choose between following edge releases and reading their notes every week, or paying for a stable channel with support. Make that choice before the first install, because swapping meshes later is a project of its own.

The install is short, and `linkerd check` guards each step:
1. `linkerd check --pre` checks the cluster.
2. You install the Gateway API CRDs yourself. Linkerd 2.20 supports Gateway API 1.2.1 to 1.5.1.
3. `linkerd install --crds | kubectl apply -f -` adds Linkerd's own CRDs.
4. `linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -` installs the control plane, and `linkerd check` waits until it is healthy.

One operational detail matters more than the rest. The trust anchor that `linkerd install` creates, the root certificate of the mesh, expires after 365 days. Linkerd's docs call a mesh with expired certificates invalid and give it a separate recovery guide. Rotating the anchor in time is work too. Every proxy has to trust the old and the new anchor side by side for a while, which takes several steps and Pod restarts. For anything that outlives a lab, create your own anchor with a longer life and write down when it expires.

sections.h: Cilium: the mesh inside the network plugin
sections.body:
Day 41 named Cilium as a network plugin (CNI) that can replace kube-proxy. Cilium does its work with eBPF: small programs that the Linux kernel runs safely as packets arrive, with no trip through a user-space proxy. Since Cilium already sits on every packet, adding mesh features to it is a short step.

Here is what Cilium does where:
- In the kernel, with eBPF: Pod networking, Service load balancing, and network policy based on an identity derived from each Pod's labels.
- In Envoy, one per node (the `cilium-envoy` DaemonSet): anything that needs HTTP, such as HTTP-aware policy, the Gateway API, GAMMA routes and L7 load balancing.
- Between nodes, encryption with WireGuard or IPsec, two standard ways to encrypt traffic between machines. That protects the wire, but it is not mTLS between workload identities.

Node encryption tells the receiver which node a packet came from. mTLS proves which workload sent it, with a certificate issued to that workload. Workload mTLS is where Cilium is still moving. Its first design, mutual authentication based on SPIFFE, is Beta and deprecated in Cilium 1.20, and the docs for the next release have removed it. The replacement runs Istio's ztunnel on each node and is also Beta. If identity-based mTLS is your main reason for a mesh, check its status before you pick Cilium for it.

Hubble is Cilium's observability layer. It records every flow the eBPF programs see. Each flow has the source and destination identity and a verdict, forwarded or dropped, plus HTTP details for traffic through Envoy. The command `hubble observe` streams flows in the terminal, and the Hubble UI draws a service map. When a NetworkPolicy drops a packet, Hubble names the Pods involved and the reason, which beats guessing.

Cilium's GAMMA support has one limit to know about. It supports only producer routes, so an HTTPRoute must live in the same namespace as the Service it attaches to.

sections.h: Consul, and a mesh that was retired
sections.body:
Consul is HashiCorp's service discovery tool, and its service mesh uses Envoy sidecars. On Kubernetes, the Helm chart installs Consul with the mesh switched on. A component called Consul Dataplane manages each Envoy, and the Consul servers hand the proxies their config over xDS. Consul's strength is reach outside Kubernetes: one mesh can include services on VMs and in several data centers. That makes it a natural pick for a company that already runs Consul for service discovery. Since August 2023 Consul has been source-available under the Business Source License. You can read the code, but the license limits how you may use it, so it is no longer open source.

AWS App Mesh, Amazon's managed mesh built on Envoy, is gone. AWS stopped taking new customers in September 2024 and ended support on September 30, 2026, after which the console and its resources are no longer available. If you find App Mesh in an old design document, read it as history, and look at ECS Service Connect for ECS workloads, which is where AWS's migration guide points.
