sections.h: GAMMA: one route for many meshes
sections.body:
Every mesh used to have its own routing objects: VirtualService in Istio, ServiceProfile and TrafficSplit in Linkerd, CiliumEnvoyConfig in Cilium. Moving to another mesh meant rewriting every route. **GAMMA**, short for Gateway API for Mesh Management and Administration, is the fix. It started in 2022, and its routes have been in the Standard channel since Gateway API 1.1.

The idea is small. On Day 44 an HTTPRoute had a Gateway as its parent, so its rules applied to traffic entering through that Gateway. In GAMMA the parent is a Service:
- `parentRefs` names the Service with `kind: Service` and `group: ""`, the core API group. Linkerd's docs and the GAMMA page write `group: core` instead; Linkerd accepts both.
- The rules apply to every meshed call to that Service, wherever the caller runs. The caller's proxy does the work, or the waypoint in Istio's ambient mode.
- Once a route is attached to a Service, requests that match none of its rules are rejected. A last rule with no `matches` catches everything else.

Where the route lives matters. A producer route sits in the Service's own namespace and applies to callers from every namespace, so the team that owns the Service writes it. A consumer route sits in the caller's namespace and changes only that caller's traffic, for example a shorter timeout for one client.

The lab shows the payoff. `mesh/linkerd/httproute-canary.yaml` has exactly the spec of Day 59's Istio route. Only the annotations differ, because Linkerd reads retries from annotations. The meshes still support different Gateway API versions: Istio 1.31's docs install 1.6.0, while Linkerd 2.20 stops at 1.5.1. So use fields that exist in the oldest version you need, and check the CRD version a cluster has before you rely on a field.

sections.h: What a mesh costs
sections.body:
A mesh is not free, and the bill has five lines:
- Latency. Every proxy adds a hop. In the worked example, one Envoy hop on the test machine added about 0.6 ms to the median call. A sidecar mesh puts two proxies on each call, one at each end.
- CPU and memory. The lab's idle Envoy, with a tiny config, held about 64 MB of memory. In sidecar mode you pay that for every Pod. By default an Istio sidecar also hears about every Service in the mesh, so its config grows with the mesh unless you limit it.
- Upgrades. The control plane and every proxy need upgrading, in a supported order. In sidecar mode a new proxy version means restarting every Pod.
- Debugging. A failed call has more places to fail. A 503 can come from the app, the caller's proxy, a waypoint or the receiver's proxy, and on-call engineers must know how to tell which.
- People. Somebody owns the certificates and the trust anchor, reads the release notes, and is the expert when the mesh is the suspect.

Istio's own numbers from Day 59 are 0.63 to 0.88 ms per call for sidecars and 0.16 to 0.20 ms for ambient mode without a waypoint. Numbers from someone else's test bench are a starting point. The worked example shows how to measure your own in five minutes, and your own are the ones to put in a decision document.

sections.h: When you do not need a mesh, and how to adopt one
sections.body:
For a handful of services owned by one team, I would not start with a mesh. Tools you already know cover most of Day 58's list:
- NetworkPolicy (Day 41) decides who may talk to whom.
- A shared client library sets timeouts and retries, such as Resilience4j in your Kotlin services.
- One Gateway (Day 44) handles TLS and routing at the edge, including canaries for traffic from users.
- OpenTelemetry (Day 57) and Prometheus (Day 50) give per-call metrics and traces.

The answer changes as services and teams multiply, when services are written in many languages, or when a customer or auditor asks for encryption and identity on every internal call. At that point one mesh is cheaper than the same work done in every repository. The lab's `CHECKLIST.md` turns this into questions you can answer for a real system.

If you adopt one, go one namespace at a time, in this order:
1. Observe. Mesh a namespace and only watch the golden metrics. You will find calls nobody knew about.
2. mTLS in permissive mode, so meshed callers encrypt and everyone else still works.
3. Strict mTLS, once the metrics show that every caller is meshed.
4. Authorization policies, starting with the services that hold sensitive data.
5. Traffic policies last: retries, timeouts, canaries and fault tests.

Multi-cluster is its own project. Istio, Linkerd and Cilium can all connect clusters, so a call can fail over to another region. Each needs certificates that all the clusters trust and network paths between them. Start it only after one cluster runs smoothly.

In a forty-floor tower, the central system wins, even though it needs a plant room, a maintenance contract and an engineer on call. Air conditioning is all or nothing once the ducts are in. A mesh can be switched on one floor at a time, in permissive mode, with the old fans still running.

# The namespace for the Linkerd lab (Day 60).
# The annotation tells Linkerd's proxy injector to add its proxy to every new Pod here.
# The apps themselves are the same as in the Istio lab: kubectl apply -f ../istio/apps.yaml

kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: hello-mesh
  annotations:
    linkerd.io/inject: enabled

code.title: mesh/linkerd/httproute-canary.yaml
code.src:
# The same canary as ../istio/httproute-canary.yaml, for Linkerd (Day 60).
# The spec is identical: this is GAMMA, the Gateway API for traffic inside a mesh.
# Only the annotations are Linkerd's own: they add retries, which Linkerd reads from
# annotations because Gateway API v1.5 has no retry field in its Standard channel.
# Linkerd 2.20 works with Gateway API v1.2.1 to v1.5.1, so install v1.5.1.
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: hello-devops-canary
  namespace: hello-mesh
  annotations:
    retry.linkerd.io/http: 5xx # retry any 5xx answer
    retry.linkerd.io/limit: "2" # at most 2 retries per request
    retry.linkerd.io/timeout: 1s # give each try 1 second
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - group: "" # "" is the core API group, where Service lives
      kind: Service
      name: hello-devops
      port: 80
  rules:
    # Rule 1: testers who send "x-canary: always" always reach the canary.
    - matches:
        - headers:
            - name: x-canary
              value: always
      backendRefs:
        - name: hello-canary
          port: 80
    # Rule 2: everyone else. About 9 in 10 requests stay on version 1.
    - backendRefs:
        - name: hello-devops
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: hello-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 10
      timeouts:
        request: 3s # give up after 3 seconds and answer 504

code.src:
# Do you need a service mesh? A checklist (Day 60)

Answer the questions in order. Stop at the first section that settles it.

## 1. Can you do without one?

You probably do not need a mesh yet if all of these are true:

- [ ] You run fewer than about ten services, owned by one or two teams.
- [ ] Most services are written in one or two languages, so a shared client library
      (for example Resilience4j on the JVM) can do retries and timeouts.
- [ ] NetworkPolicies (Day 41) already limit which Pods may talk to which.
- [ ] One Gateway (Day 44) handles TLS and routing for traffic from outside.
- [ ] OpenTelemetry (Day 57) and Prometheus (Day 50) already show you per-service errors
      and latency.
- [ ] No auditor or customer requires encryption and identity on every internal call.

If you ticked every box, write down what would change your mind and revisit in six months.

## 2. What would a mesh give you that you lack today?

Tick the ones you need now, not some day:

- [ ] mTLS between every pair of services, with identities you can write policy about
- [ ] The same golden metrics (requests, errors, latency) for every service, with no code
- [ ] Traffic splitting for canaries between services inside the cluster
- [ ] Retries, timeouts and circuit breaking set the same way for every language
- [ ] Authorization by caller identity and HTTP path
- [ ] Traffic between several clusters

No ticks: go back to section 1. One or two ticks: check whether a smaller tool covers them
(Cilium as your CNI, a client library, cert-manager). Three or more: read on.

## 3. Which one?

- Linkerd: you want mTLS and golden metrics with the fewest moving parts, and you are
  fine with sidecars. Check the release model: open source edge releases, or a vendor
  distribution for stable releases.
- Istio, ambient mode: you want the widest feature set (fault injection, rich routing,
  egress control, VMs) with no sidecars, and you can start with L4 only.
- Istio, sidecar mode: as above, when you need a feature that ambient mode does not
  support yet, or multi-cluster support at the Stable level.
- Cilium: you already use Cilium as the CNI, or want to, and your L7 needs are modest.
  Check the status of the mTLS features you need: some are still beta.
- Consul: you have many services outside Kubernetes (VMs) and already run Consul.

## 4. Can you afford it?

- [ ] Someone owns the mesh: upgrades, certificates, incidents. Name the person or team.
- [ ] You have measured the latency and memory it adds, on your own traffic.
- [ ] You have a plan for upgrades. In sidecar mode, every Pod restarts to get the new proxy.
- [ ] You know where the trust anchor lives and when it expires.
- [ ] On-call engineers can tell a 503 from the proxy from a 503 from the app.

## 5. Roll it out in steps

1. Install it in a test cluster and mesh one namespace. Watch the metrics only.
2. Mesh more namespaces with mTLS in permissive mode (plain text still allowed).
3. Check that every caller of a service is meshed, then switch that namespace to strict.
4. Add authorization policies, starting with "deny nothing, log everything" where the
   mesh supports an audit mode.
5. Only now add traffic policies: retries, timeouts, canaries, fault injection tests.

lessons.mistake: Installing a mesh to fix a problem it cannot fix is an expensive way to learn what a mesh does. A mesh will not speed up a slow database query or stop an app from crashing on bad input; it only wraps proxies around the slow call. Write down the two or three problems you expect it to solve, measure them before and after, and take it out again if the numbers do not move.
lessons.real_world: An auditor asks a payments company to encrypt every internal call, and the request lands on the platform team. They check what already exists, find NetworkPolicies and OpenTelemetry in place, and adopt Linkerd for mTLS and golden metrics only, with no traffic rules at first. When canaries between services become routine a year later, they add HTTPRoutes in the GAMMA form, so the routes would survive a move to another mesh.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences when you would add a service mesh and which one you would try first. Mention cost, mTLS and GAMMA.
explain_back.answer: I would add a mesh when many services in several languages need the same mTLS, metrics and traffic rules. An auditor who requires encryption and identity on every internal call is another good reason. For a few services, NetworkPolicy, client-side retries, one Gateway and OpenTelemetry are cheaper. Every mesh costs latency per hop, memory per proxy, upgrades and people, so I would measure those first. I would try Linkerd for mTLS and golden metrics, or Istio in ambient mode for a wider feature set, and write routes as GAMMA HTTPRoutes so they move with me.

recap: Linkerd uses its own Rust sidecar proxy and gives mTLS and golden metrics with almost no config.
The Linkerd project ships edge releases; stable releases come from vendors such as Buoyant, free under 50 employees.
Cilium handles L3 and L4 in eBPF and runs one Envoy per node for HTTP; its workload mTLS is still Beta.
GAMMA attaches HTTPRoutes to a Service, so one route file works in Istio, Linkerd and Cilium.
A mesh costs latency, memory, upgrades, debugging time and people. Measure before you decide.
Adopt in steps: observe, permissive mTLS, strict mTLS, authorization, then traffic rules.

check.q: Your cluster runs Cilium as its CNI. A team wants a 95/5 canary between two internal services. Which object is the most portable way to write it?
options: A CiliumEnvoyConfig with weighted clusters
An Istio VirtualService with two destinations
An HTTPRoute whose parentRef is the Service
A NetworkPolicy with two ingress rules
check.why: A GAMMA HTTPRoute works in Cilium today and in Istio and Linkerd too.

check.q: A team installs Linkerd with the default `linkerd install` and never touches its certificates. What breaks first, a year later?
options: The Gateway API CRDs expire
The default trust anchor and issuer expire
The edge release stops receiving traffic
The proxies run out of memory
check.why: The default trust anchor and issuer certificate last a year; without rotation, the proxies can no longer get valid certificates.

check.q: Which situation is the weakest reason to add a service mesh?
options: One slow SQL query makes the checkout page slow
An auditor requires authenticated, encrypted calls everywhere
Forty services in five languages need the same retry rules
Every team wants per-route success rates without code
check.why: A mesh can show you the slow call, but it cannot make the query faster.

interview.q: How do Istio, Linkerd and Cilium differ as service meshes?
interview.a: Istio uses Envoy, either as a sidecar in every Pod or, in ambient mode, as an optional waypoint behind a per-node ztunnel, and it has the widest feature set. Linkerd uses its own small Rust sidecar and focuses on mTLS, golden metrics and reliability with very little configuration. Cilium builds the mesh into its network plugin: eBPF in the kernel for L3 and L4, one Envoy per node for HTTP, and Hubble for flow visibility. Its workload mTLS is still Beta. All three accept Gateway API routes, which makes the routing layer portable.

interview.q: When would you not use a service mesh?
interview.a: With only a few services and teams, a shared client library, NetworkPolicies, an ingress Gateway and OpenTelemetry cover retries, segmentation, edge TLS and visibility for less. A mesh adds latency to every call, memory for every proxy, upgrades and one more system to debug. I would also wait when nobody can own it, because certificates and upgrades need a named owner. I revisit the decision when the number of services, languages or compliance demands grows.

interview.q: How would you roll out a mesh in an existing cluster?
interview.a: Namespace by namespace, in layers. First I mesh one namespace and use only the metrics, which usually shows dependencies nobody knew about. Then I turn on mTLS in permissive mode, check that every caller is meshed, and switch to strict. Authorization policies come next and traffic policies such as retries and canaries last. At each step I keep a way back, such as removing the namespace label, and I watch the error rates.

deeper.body:
If you want to see the eBPF side for yourself, Cilium runs on kind as long as kind does not install its own network plugin. This is outside the graded lab, and none of it was run in the course's test environment, so follow the Cilium docs when a step has changed:
1. Create a kind cluster from a config that sets `disableDefaultCNI: true` under `networking`. Its nodes stay NotReady until Cilium is installed, which is expected.
2. Install the CLIs with `brew install cilium-cli hubble`.
3. Run `cilium install`, then `cilium status --wait`.
4. Turn on Hubble with `cilium hubble enable`, and check it with `hubble status -P`. The `-P` flag opens a port-forward to Hubble for you.
5. Deploy `mesh/istio/apps.yaml`, add a deny-all NetworkPolicy like Day 41's to its namespace, and run `hubble observe -P --verdict DROPPED`.

Each dropped flow shows source and destination with their Cilium identities and the reason. Remove the policy and watch the same flows turn into FORWARDED.

Why bother if you are not choosing Cilium? Because Hubble shows the layer under every mesh. Istio's ztunnel and Linkerd's proxy both ride on the network plugin, and when a call fails before any proxy sees it, the network plugin is where you look. On a cluster that already runs Cilium, Hubble plus NetworkPolicies may be all the visibility and segmentation you need, which is the no-mesh answer from today's checklist.

Two cautions from the docs. GAMMA in Cilium needs kube-proxy replacement turned on, so a default install may not be enough for HTTPRoutes; read the [GAMMA page](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/servicemesh/gateway-api/gamma/) first. And if you ever run Linkerd on top of Cilium, read Linkerd's cluster configuration page. Cilium's socket-level load balancing can bypass part of Linkerd's routing, and the page lists the Cilium setting to change.

On workload mTLS, read the status line at the top of each page before you plan anything. The [mutual authentication page](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/servicemesh/mutual-authentication/mutual-authentication/) for 1.20 says Beta, and so does the newer [ztunnel encryption page](https://docs.cilium.io/en/latest/security/network/encryption-ztunnel/).

recap: A service mesh moves timeouts, retries, mTLS, traffic splits and per-call metrics out of app code and into proxies.
In Envoy, listeners accept connections, the HTTP connection manager runs filters, routes pick clusters and clusters pick endpoints.
Health checks probe hosts, outlier detection watches real answers, and circuit breakers fail fast.
A control plane sends Envoy its config over xDS; the admin port shows what each proxy really has.
Istio is istiod plus either a sidecar per Pod or ambient mode: ztunnel per node and waypoints for HTTP.
Workload identity comes from ServiceAccounts as SPIFFE IDs. Go PERMISSIVE, then STRICT, then add AuthorizationPolicies.
Linkerd has a Rust sidecar and automatic mTLS; the project ships edge releases and vendors ship stable ones.
Cilium does L3 and L4 in eBPF, runs Envoy per node for HTTP, and shows flows in Hubble.
GAMMA HTTPRoutes attach to a Service and work across meshes.
Measure what a mesh costs, and skip it while a few services do fine without one.

flashcards.front: Which five problems between services does a mesh handle?
flashcards.back: Timeouts, retries, encryption with identity (mTLS), traffic splitting and per-call metrics.

flashcards.front: Data plane or control plane: which one carries user traffic?
flashcards.back: The data plane, made of the proxies. The control plane only configures them and signs their certificates.

flashcards.front: Name Envoy's core objects in the order a request meets them.
flashcards.back: Listener, HTTP connection manager with its filters, route, cluster, endpoint.

flashcards.front: What do LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS and SDS send to Envoy?
flashcards.back: Listeners, route tables, clusters, endpoints and secrets (certificates and keys).

flashcards.front: How does an active health check differ from outlier detection?
flashcards.back: A health check sends its own probe request. Outlier detection watches real answers and ejects hosts that keep failing.

flashcards.front: Why does a two-host Envoy cluster never eject a host with default settings?
flashcards.back: `max_ejection_percent` defaults to 10%, which is less than one of two hosts.

flashcards.front: How does a sidecar catch the app's traffic without code changes?
flashcards.back: iptables rules in the Pod's network send connections to the proxy. Istio uses port 15001 out and 15006 in.

flashcards.front: What is a Kubernetes native sidecar?
flashcards.back: An init container with `restartPolicy: Always`. It starts before the app and stops after it; stable since Kubernetes 1.33.

flashcards.front: In Istio ambient mode, what do ztunnel and a waypoint each do?
flashcards.back: ztunnel, one per node, does mTLS and L4 policy. A waypoint, an Envoy per namespace or service, does HTTP routing and L7 policy.

flashcards.front: Which namespace label joins Istio in each mode?
flashcards.back: Sidecar: `istio-injection=enabled`, then restart the Pods. Ambient: `istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient`, no restart.

flashcards.front: What is the SPIFFE ID of ServiceAccount `client` in namespace `shop`?
flashcards.back: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/client, with the default trust domain.

flashcards.front: PERMISSIVE or STRICT: which one still accepts plain text?
flashcards.back: PERMISSIVE accepts mTLS and plain text. STRICT accepts only mTLS.

flashcards.front: What happens once an ALLOW AuthorizationPolicy selects a workload?
flashcards.back: Every request that no ALLOW rule matches is refused with 403 `RBAC: access denied`.
Vendors, mainly Buoyant Enterprise for Linkerd. The open source project ships edge releases.

flashcards.front: Where does Cilium handle HTTP features?
flashcards.back: In an Envoy proxy that runs once per node. eBPF in the kernel covers L3 and L4.

flashcards.front: What makes an HTTPRoute a GAMMA route?
flashcards.back: Its parentRef is a Service (`kind: Service`, core group) instead of a Gateway.

quiz.q: Envoy splits traffic 90/10 between two clusters, but over 100 requests you count 84 and 16. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The weights are broken and must add up to 1000
The cluster is chosen at random per request, so small samples vary
Envoy splits by connection, not by request
Health checks moved traffic to the canary
quiz.why: Weighted clusters are picked at random for each request, and the shares only settle near 90/10 over many requests.

quiz.q: Which xDS API carries the data that changes most often in a busy Kubernetes cluster?
options: LDS
CDS
EDS
SDS
quiz.why: EDS carries the Pod IPs behind each cluster, which change with every rollout and scaling event.

quiz.q: A Pod in an ambient namespace needs an AuthorizationPolicy that matches HTTP paths. What must exist for it to work?
options: A sidecar container in that same Pod
A NetworkPolicy that allows port 15008
An Istio Gateway in istio-system
A waypoint that the policy targets
quiz.why: ztunnel cannot read paths; only a waypoint can enforce HTTP rules, and the policy attaches to it with `targetRefs`.

quiz.q: You switch a namespace to PeerAuthentication STRICT. Which caller breaks?
options: A Pod in a namespace that is not in the mesh
A meshed Pod in another namespace
A meshed Pod in the same namespace
A meshed Pod that uses the default ServiceAccount
quiz.why: STRICT refuses plain text, and only callers outside the mesh still send it.

quiz.q: Which command shows whether the connections between Linkerd workloads are encrypted?
options: linkerd check --pre
linkerd install --crds
linkerd viz edges
kubectl get pods -o wide
quiz.why: `linkerd viz edges` lists the connections between workloads with a SECURED column.

quiz.q: An HTTPRoute is attached to Service `orders` with one rule that matches only `/api`. A meshed client calls `/health` on `orders`. What does GAMMA say happens?
options: The call goes to `orders` as if no route existed
The call is rejected, because it matches no rule
The call goes to the first backend of the route
The mesh retries it until a rule matches
quiz.why: Once routes are attached to a Service, requests that match none of their rules are rejected.

quiz.q: Which cost of sidecar mode does ambient mode avoid?
options: Restarting every Pod to upgrade the proxy
Running a control plane
Installing the Gateway API CRDs
Issuing certificates for mTLS
quiz.why: In ambient mode the proxies run outside the app Pods, so upgrading them does not restart your apps.

quiz.q: Which situation is the strongest reason to skip a mesh for now?
options: An auditor requires mTLS on every internal call
Thirty services in four languages need the same retry rules
Teams want canaries between internal services every week
Six services, one team, with NetworkPolicies and OpenTelemetry in place
quiz.why: A few services with segmentation and telemetry already in place get little from a mesh but pay all its costs.

quiz.q: You turn on mesh retries for 5xx answers on every route. Which call does that make risky?
options: GET /orders/42 to read one order
PUT /orders/42 with the full order
POST /payments that charges a card
DELETE /orders/42 to cancel it
quiz.why: POST is not idempotent, so a retry after a timeout can charge the card twice unless the API uses idempotency keys.

quiz.q: kube-proxy balances per connection. A gRPC client keeps one connection open to a Service with three Pods. What does an L7 mesh proxy change?
options: Nothing, because the connection still pins one Pod
It balances each request across the Pods
It opens a new TCP connection for every request
It turns the Service into a headless one
quiz.why: An L7 proxy sees each request on the connection and can send each one to a different endpoint.
